hints: Start by thinking what allele frequency means - the proportion of each version of a gene in a gene pool - and what kinds of events could add, remove or reshuffle those versions.
Think about the only process that can create a completely new allele by changing the DNA base sequence.
Think about changes that are random and not linked to advantage, which are especially powerful when only a few individuals breed.
Think about two special cases of small populations - a few individuals starting a new isolated colony, and a large population suddenly crashing to very few survivors.
Think about the non-random process where the environment favours one phenotype, so individuals with those alleles survive and reproduce more.
Think about movement of individuals or gametes between populations, and reshuffling of existing alleles during meiosis.
walkthrough:
New Alleles From Mutation**
Think of the gene pool as a bag of alleles. Only mutation puts a brand new allele into the bag by a random change in DNA base sequence, for example by substitution or deletion. This can increase frequency of a new allele from zero.

Random Change In Small Populations**
Genetic drift is random fluctuation in allele frequencies due to chance in which individuals survive and reproduce. It does not need an advantage. Two extreme forms are the founder effect, where a small group splits off to found a new isolated population, and the bottleneck effect, where a disaster or disease causes a large fall in numbers so survivors carry only a sample of alleles.

Selection, Movement And Reshuffling**
Natural, directional or disruptive selection is non-random: individuals with advantageous alleles are more likely to survive and pass them on, so those frequencies rise. Migration or gene flow adds or removes alleles when individuals move and interbreed between populations. Finally, genetic recombination including crossing over in meiosis creates new combinations of alleles, changing their associations in gametes.

Final answer: Any six: mutation creates new alleles; genetic drift is random change in allele frequency; founder effect where small group separates to found new population with unrepresentative frequencies; bottleneck effect where large fall in population leaves unrepresentative survivors; natural / directional / disruptive selection changes frequencies; migration / gene flow / interbreeding between populations; genetic recombination / crossing over breaks linkage groups.

hints: Think about what genotype gives uniform height - all plants need the same alleles - and how repeated self-pollination between close relatives would change homozygosity.
Think about why breeders first make two separate pure-breeding lines rather than selecting directly for vigour.
Think about what happens when you cross those two different pure lines together and what genotype and phenotype the F1 offspring will all share.
walkthrough:
Make Pure Lines By Inbreeding**
Uniform height means all plants have the same genotype for height genes. Breeders repeatedly inbreed or self-pollinate selected plants for several generations. This increases homozygosity and produces homozygous pure-breeding lines, one line for each desired trait.

Cross Lines To Make Hybrids**
Then breeders carry out outbreeding or hybridisation by crossing two different homozygous lines together. For example, pollen from one pure line is used to pollinate flowers of the other pure line.

Heterozygous Vigorous Uniform F1**
All the F1 offspring receive one allele from each parent, so they are all genetically identical heterozygotes with increased heterozygosity. This gives hybrid vigour, so plants are vigorous, large and healthy, and because they all share the same genotype they grow to uniform height for easy harvest.

Final answer: Inbreeding by self-pollination over generations to produce homozygous pure lines; outbreeding / hybridisation by crossing two different homozygous lines; F1 hybrids are all heterozygous, showing hybrid vigour and uniform height.
